q: A pilot who needs highly detailed data on individual plants should generally fly at:
options: A lower altitude and slower speed
A higher altitude and faster speed
The same altitude regardless of the goal
Only at night
explain: Lower altitude and slower speed capture more detail per image, which is important for highly detailed, individual-plant-level data.

q: Why should missions collecting spectral imagery be flown around solar noon?
options: The drone's battery charges faster in direct sun
It ensures consistent lighting conditions across the mission
It avoids interference from other aircraft
It is required by FAA regulation
explain: Flying around solar noon (10 AM–2 PM) with minimal cloud cover keeps lighting conditions consistent, which matters for reliable spectral data.

q: What must be collected when a Ground Control Point (GCP) is placed in a field?
options: Its color
Its GPS position
Its weight
Its temperature
explain: The GCP's GPS position must be recorded so it can be used to align images accurately during stitching.

q: Where should GCPs generally be placed in a field?
options: Only in the exact center of the field
Randomly, location does not matter
Only outside the field boundary
In the corners of the area of interest, and potentially throughout the field
explain: GCPs should be placed in the corners of the area of interest, and potentially in additional locations throughout the field depending on its size.

q: When is color correction especially useful?
options: Only for very short flights
Only when flying at night
During long flights where lighting conditions may change, or when comparing flights from different times
Color correction is never necessary for drone imagery
explain: Color correction helps account for shifting lighting conditions during long flights, or when comparing imagery captured at different points in time.

q: What coordinate system do drones typically use by default to record image position?
options: UTM
RTK
GCP
WGS84
explain: Drones typically record position using WGS84, a global coordinate system based on longitude, latitude, and elevation.

q: Why can WGS84 introduce error during high-precision stitching?
options: The real-world distance covered by one degree of longitude changes with latitude
It only works during daylight hours
It cannot record elevation data
It is not compatible with any drone sensors
explain: Because the distance between degrees of longitude narrows moving away from the equator, WGS84's degree-based measurements aren't spatially consistent everywhere, introducing error in high-precision work.

q: What does the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) system provide that WGS84 alone does not?
options: A grid system with standardized, highly precise measurements
Automatic color correction
A way to fly the drone remotely
Faster image processing
explain: UTM projects a standardized grid across the globe, giving consistent, highly precise positioning that helps overcome WGS84's distance inconsistency.

q: What does an RTK (Real-Time Kinematic) system add to a drone's positioning?
options: Longer battery life
The ability to fly without a remote controller
Enhanced precision and accuracy using satellite-based projected coordinate systems
Automatic image stitching
explain: RTK tools use projected coordinate systems and satellites to significantly enhance the precision and accuracy of each image's recorded position.
